contradiction.viewer_thinks: a fever is the body overheating out of control — the heat is the illness
contradiction.actually: the brain deliberately raises the set point and the body defends that higher temperature

beats.narration: You are burning hot — and shivering under a blanket. A fever is not your body losing control of its temperature. It is your body choosing a new one.
beats.claim: fever is a regulated rise of the body's temperature set point, orchestrated by the brain
beats.visual_question: why do you shiver while burning hot?
beats.visual_answer: a cutaway figure glows from the core while the skin surface shows shiver marks — heat inside, chills outside

beats.narration: Deep at the base of your brain sits the hypothalamus — the body's thermostat. In a fever it does not fail. It is recalibrated.
beats.claim: the hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat for core temperature
beats.visual_question: where does the body keep its thermostat?
beats.visual_answer: a cutaway head profile with the hypothalamus lit deep at the brain's base, baseline dial beside it

beats.narration: Immune cells in your blood release chemical messengers. They reach the brain and trigger prostaglandin E two — which pushes the thermostat's set point up, one or two degrees.
beats.claim: pyrogenic cytokines induce prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, raising the set point
beats.visual_question: what physically moves the set point?
beats.visual_answer: cytokine dots travel a vessel into the hypothalamus and the set-point dial turns from 37 to 39

beats.narration: Your core now sits below the new target — so you feel cold. Skin vessels clamp down, and you shiver: muscles cranking out heat until the body meets the number it set.
beats.claim: vasoconstriction and shivering raise core temperature toward the raised set point
beats.visual_question: how does the body climb to the new set point?
beats.visual_answer: narrowed skin vessels, zigzag shiver marks on muscles and inward heat arrows to the core

beats.narration: The fever itself is part of the defense. Higher temperatures slow many pathogens and speed immune cells — though very high fevers harm, and the balance is still debated.
beats.claim: moderate fever can slow pathogens and support immunity; very high fever harms; net benefit is debated
beats.visual_question: what does the higher temperature buy?
beats.visual_answer: bacterial chains replicating slowly beside a brisker immune cell — the trade-off shown, not hidden

beats.narration: When the infection quiets — or an ibuprofen tablet blocks the prostaglandins — the set point falls back. Now you are too hot. Vessels open, and sweat evaporates to dump the excess.
beats.claim: antipyretics inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; the falling set point drives vasodilation and sweating
beats.visual_question: why does the fever break with sweat?
beats.visual_answer: the dial unwinds to baseline, wide-open skin vessels glow and sweat beads lift off the skin surface

beats.narration: The chills were the climb. The sweat is the descent. A fever is your own thermostat, aimed higher on purpose — and your body fighting to reach the target it set.
beats.claim: fever symptoms follow the set-point trajectory: chills on the ramp, sweat on the descent
beats.visual_question: what was the whole loop for?
beats.visual_answer: the resolved cutaway: dial at baseline, calm core gradient, open vessels — the regulation story closed in one frame

visual_contradiction.seems: a fever is your body overheating out of control — the heat IS the illness
visual_contradiction.actually: the brain deliberately raises the set point and the body defends that higher temperature
visual_contradiction.reveal: the cutaway head shows the set-point dial turning up while the body actively heats itself toward the new target

payoff_image.image: the cutaway figure at rest — dial back at baseline, open glowing vessels and a calm core gradient: the whole regulation loop resolved in one frame
